newsitem.title: USA: Eight states oppose Staples merger.
newsitem.headline: Eight states oppose Staples merger.

text.p: Eight states joined to file court papers Friday opposing the $4 billion merger of office superstore chains Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. as a bad deal for consumers.

The attorneys general of California, Illinois, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Washington were filing a "friend of the court" brief with U.S. District Judge Thomas Hogan, who was considering whether to grant a preliminary injunction that would effectively halt the merger.

New York state Attorney General Dennis Vacco, a Democrat, said his investigation had "shown that competition between the two companies results in lower prices for New York consumers" and that a merger would increase prices.
The Republican attorney general of Pennsylvania, Mike Fisher, echoed those views.
"It is our belief that this proposed merger would eliminate competition and result in higher prices for consumers," he said in a statement.
The eight attorneys general are backing the views of the Federal Trade Commission, which last week spent five days presenting evidence in federal court.
The attorneys general say Staples and Office Depot claim that "a merger of direct competitors whose business strategy depends on high volume and 'low' prices will introduce competition."
The eight states argue the claim is "wholly at odds with the concept of competition embodied in the antitrust laws."

The states argue the only way to keep prices low for consumers at Office Depot and Staples is through "competitive prices and ... all the other benefits that flow from competition within the unique competitive arena which the office supply superstores represent."
But the lead attorney for Staples and Office Depot took vigorous exception to their views.

"In this case, it is the unthinking antitrust inside-aficionados that are 'wholly at odds,' not only with sound antitrust policy but with common sense as well," said Don Kempf in a telephone interview.

Kempf said the eight attorneys general had "elevated their fascination with untested new theories over the real-world reality that this merger will serve consumers well by providing them -- directly -- with lower prices than either Staples or Office Depot could provide on a stand-alone basis."
The FTC and Staples will present their final oral arguments Thursday before Judge Hogan, who has said he will rule in the middle of next month.
